waalo.s: Waalo was a Wolof kingdom in the lower Senegal River valley in present-day Senegal. According to tradition, Ndiadiane Ndiaye unified Waalo, Cayor, Baol, Sine and other Wolof-speaking states into a loose confederation centred on Jolof.

wadai-empire.s: The Wadai Empire was a Muslim sultanate in the eastern Sahel, in what is now eastern Chad, founded around 1611 when Abd al-Karim overthrew the Tunjur rulers. Its capital was initially at Wara.

wadi-al-ajal.s: The Wadi al-Ajal is a valley in the Fezzan region of south-western Libya, and the heartland of the Garamantian Empire. The Garamantian Empire profile explains that the Garamantes irrigated it through a foggara network of underground canals.

wadi-ash-shati.s: The Wadi ash-Shati is a valley in the Fezzan region of south-western Libya. The Garamantian Empire profile names it, alongside the Wadi al-Ajal, among the habitable niches of the Fezzan where the Garamantes settled.

wahrez.s: Wahrez was a Sasanian Persian general of the late sixth century CE. The Aksumite Empire profile records that around 575–578 CE a Sasanian expeditionary force under Wahrez defeated the Aksumite garrison at Sana'a in Yemen and installed a Persian governor.

walashma-dynasty.s: The Walashma dynasty was a Muslim ruling family of the Horn of Africa that governed the Ifat Sultanate and then the Adal Sultanate. After Ifat's defeat by Ethiopia around 1410, Sabr ad-Din III re-established the dynasty's state at Zeila around 1415, founding Adal.

walata.s: Walata, or Oualata, is an oasis town in south-eastern Mauritania that was an important terminus of trans-Saharan caravan routes. The nearby escarpment of Dhar Walata is associated with the Tichitt culture from which the Ghana Empire emerged.

walls-of-benin.s: The Walls of Benin were an extensive system of earthworks consisting of ramparts and ditches surrounding Benin City and the surrounding countryside, in present-day southern Nigeria. Built over several centuries, they are among the largest earthworks in the world.

walls-of-constantinople.s: The Walls of Constantinople were the fortifications protecting the Byzantine capital, above all the land walls known as the Theodosian Walls, completed in 413 CE. Their triple line of moat, outer wall and inner wall made the city almost impregnable for centuries.

wang-anshi.s: Wang Anshi was a Chinese statesman and chancellor of the Northern Song Dynasty in the eleventh century. He introduced a sweeping programme of reforms, the New Policies, including state loans to farmers, changes to taxation and labour service, and reorganisation of the militia.

wangara.s: The Wangara, also known as the Dyula, were Mande-speaking Muslim merchants of West Africa who organised long-distance trade in gold, kola nuts, salt and other goods. They established trading communities across the region.

war-elephant.s: A war elephant is an elephant trained for combat, used to charge enemy formations, carry archers and intimidate opponents. They were especially important in Indian warfare, notably in the Maurya and Gupta empires, and spread to the Hellenistic world through the Seleucid Empire.

war-guilt-clause.s: The War Guilt Clause, Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles of 1919, required Germany to accept responsibility for the loss and damage caused by the First World War. It provided the legal basis for reparations.

war-of-the-golden-stool.s: The War of the Golden Stool was an Ashanti uprising against British rule in 1900, also known as the Yaa Asantewaa War. It was provoked when the British governor demanded to sit on the Golden Stool, the sacred symbol of Ashanti nationhood.

war-of-the-spanish-succession.s: The War of the Spanish Succession was a European conflict fought from 1701 to 1714 over who should inherit the Spanish throne after the death of the childless Charles II. France supported the Bourbon claimant Philip of Anjou, while Britain, the Dutch Republic and Austria…

war-reparations.s: War reparations are payments imposed on a defeated state to compensate the victors for the costs and damage of war. The Treaty of Apamea of 188 BCE required the Seleucid Empire to pay 15,000 talents in reparations to Rome.

wara.s: Wara was the first capital of the Wadai Empire, in the east of present-day Chad. The Wadai Empire profile records that Abd al-Karim established his Islamic sultanate there around 1611 after overthrowing the Tunjur rulers.

wars-of-the-diadochi.s: The Wars of the Diadochi were the conflicts fought between Alexander the Great's generals, the Diadochi or successors, for control of his empire after his death, lasting from 323 to 281 BCE. They ended the unity of the Macedonian Empire.

warsaw.s: Warsaw is the capital of Poland, on the Vistula River. It became the royal residence and effective capital of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth after Sigismund III Vasa moved the court there from Kraków around 1596, and from 1569 it was the regular seat of the Sejm and of…

warsaw-confederation.s: The Warsaw Confederation was an act adopted by the nobility of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1573 that guaranteed religious peace and freedom among the nobility. The Commonwealth profile notes that it protected Catholics, Lutherans, Calvinists and Orthodox Christians…

wasashatta.s: Wasashatta was a king of Hanigalbat, the rump of the Mitanni state, in the thirteenth century BCE. The Mitanni Empire profile records that rebellions led by Shattuara I and Wasashatta against Assyrian domination were suppressed by the Assyrian kings Adad-nirari I and…

washukanni.s: Washukanni was the capital of the Mitanni Empire, probably located in the Khabur valley of north-eastern Syria, though its exact site has not been confirmed. The Mitanni Empire profile records that it was sacked by the Hittite king Suppiluliuma I around 1340 BCE.

wazir.s: Wazir is a variant spelling of vizier, the title of a chief minister. In the Sikh Empire it was the title of the prime minister at the Lahore Darbar, the imperial court.

wei-qing.s: Wei Qing was a Han Dynasty general of the second century BCE who led major campaigns against the Xiongnu under Emperor Wu. With his nephew Huo Qubing, he conducted the decisive northern campaigns that drove Xiongnu power beyond the Gobi Desert.

wei-zheng.s: Wei Zheng was a statesman and adviser of the early Tang Dynasty, famous as the remonstrance official of Emperor Taizong. The Tang Dynasty profile notes that Taizong famously accepted Wei Zheng's blunt criticisms.

weimar-republic.s: The Weimar Republic was the democratic German state established after the fall of the German Empire in 1918, named after the city where its constitution was drafted. It faced the burdens of the Treaty of Versailles, reparations, hyperinflation and the Great Depression.

weisuo-system.s: The weisuo system was the military organisation of the Ming Empire, under which hereditary soldier households were assigned to garrisons called wei and smaller units called suo. The garrisons were expected to support themselves through military farmland.

well.s: A well is a shaft dug into the ground to reach water, essential for life and travel in arid regions such as the Sahara and the Sahel. Control of wells determined which routes caravans and armies could use.

west-africa.s: West Africa is the western region of the African continent, stretching from the Sahara to the Gulf of Guinea. It was home to a succession of powerful states, including the Ghana, Mali and Songhai empires of the Sahel, the forest kingdoms of Benin, Oyo and Ashanti, and the…

west-francia.s: West Francia was the western kingdom created by the division of the Carolingian Empire at the Treaty of Verdun in 843 CE, assigned to Charles the Bald. It roughly corresponded to the western and central parts of modern France.

western-europe.s: Western Europe is the western part of the European continent. The Carolingian Empire unified much of it under Charlemagne around 800 CE.

western-ghats.s: The Western Ghats are a mountain range running parallel to the western coast of the Indian peninsula. Their rugged terrain and hill forts provided the base of Maratha power.

western-jin-dynasty.s: The Western Jin dynasty was a Chinese dynasty that ruled from 265 to 316 CE, founded by the Sima family, which seized power from the Wei state. It briefly reunified China in 280 CE, ending the Three Kingdoms period.

western-roman-empire.s: The Western Roman Empire was the western half of the Roman Empire, governed separately after the permanent division of 395 CE. Weakened by fiscal crisis, civil wars and Germanic invasions, it lost North Africa to the Vandals and saw Rome sacked in 410 and 455.

western-satraps.s: The Western Satraps were a dynasty of Saka (Indo-Scythian) rulers who governed western India, including Gujarat and Malwa, from around the first to the fourth century CE. They controlled important ports and trade routes.

western-sudan.s: The Western Sudan is a historical term for the Sahel and savannah region of West Africa south of the Sahara, from the Atlantic to around Lake Chad. It was the home of the Ghana, Mali and Songhai empires, whose wealth rested on gold and trans-Saharan trade.

western-turkic-khaganate.s: The Western Turkic Khaganate was the western half of the Gokturk Empire, which became a separate state after the empire divided in the late sixth century. It controlled the steppes and oasis cities of Central Asia along the Silk Road.

western-wei.s: The Western Wei was a northern Chinese state that ruled from 535 to 557 CE, one of the successors to the Northern Wei dynasty. The Gokturk Empire profile notes that the Turkic leader Bumin allied with Western Wei and married a Wei princess.

westminster-system.s: The Westminster system is the model of parliamentary government developed in the United Kingdom, in which the executive is drawn from and accountable to an elected legislature. It includes a ceremonial head of state, a prime minister and cabinet, and an official opposition.

wet-rice-agriculture.s: Wet-rice agriculture is the cultivation of rice in flooded paddy fields, a highly productive system that can support dense populations. It relies on careful control of water through irrigation, embankments and reservoirs.

white-lotus.s: The White Lotus was a Chinese religious tradition combining Buddhist and popular beliefs with expectations of the coming of the Maitreya Buddha. Its millenarian teachings inspired repeated rebellions against ruling dynasties.

white-lotus-rebellion.s: The White Lotus Rebellion was a large uprising in central China from 1796 to 1804, inspired by White Lotus millenarian teachings and fuelled by poverty, population pressure and official corruption. It took years and great expense for the Qing to suppress.

wilhelm-i.s: Wilhelm I was King of Prussia from 1861 and the first emperor of the German Empire from 1871 until his death in 1888. With his chancellor Otto von Bismarck, he presided over the wars against Denmark, Austria and France that united Germany under Prussian leadership.

wilhelm-ii.s: Wilhelm II was the last German Emperor and King of Prussia, reigning from 1888 until his abdication in 1918. After dismissing Bismarck he pursued an assertive world policy, including a large naval programme that alienated Britain.

wind-of-change-speech.s: The Wind of Change speech was an address delivered by the British prime minister Harold Macmillan to the parliament of South Africa in Cape Town in 1960. He acknowledged the strength of African national consciousness and signalled that Britain would not resist decolonisation.

wismar.s: Wismar is a Baltic port town in northern Germany. Under the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, Sweden received Wismar along with the bishoprics of Bremen and Verden and part of Pomerania.

w-adys-aw-ii-jagie-o.s: Władysław II Jagiełło, known in Lithuanian as Jogaila, was Grand Duke of Lithuania who became King of Poland after marrying Queen Jadwiga under the Union of Krewo of 1385. He founded the Jagiellonian dynasty and led the joint Polish-Lithuanian victory over the Teutonic Order…

w-adys-aw-iv-vasa.s: Władysław IV Vasa was King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania from 1632 to 1648. In his youth he was elected Tsar of Russia after Polish forces occupied Moscow in 1610, though he never ruled there.

w-adys-aw-sicinski.s: Władysław Siciński was a deputy to the Sejm of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. In 1652 he dissolved the entire Sejm by his solitary objection, the first successful exercise of the liberum veto.

wola.s: Wola is an area on the western outskirts of historic Warsaw, now a district of the city. In the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, the field of Wola was the site of royal elections.

wollo.s: Wollo is a historical province in north-central Ethiopia. It was the region most severely affected by the famine of 1973–1974.

wollo-famine.s: The Wollo famine was a severe famine in the Wollo region of Ethiopia in 1973–1974 that killed many thousands of people. The imperial government initially denied and concealed its scale.

wolof.s: The Wolof are a West African people of present-day Senegal and The Gambia, whose language is widely spoken across the region. Several Wolof-speaking states, including Waalo, Cayor, Baol and Jolof, were united in a confederation centred on Jolof.

woodblock-printing.s: Woodblock printing is a technique of printing text or images by carving them in relief on a wooden block, inking it and pressing paper onto it. It developed in China and was in use under the Tang Dynasty, which produced some of the earliest surviving printed texts, including…

woodrow-wilson.s: Woodrow Wilson was President of the United States from 1913 to 1921, who led the country into the First World War in 1917. His Fourteen Points of 1918 promoted national self-determination as a principle for the post-war settlement.

wu-sangui.s: Wu Sangui was a Ming general who commanded the defences at Shanhai Pass in 1644. After rebels captured Beijing, he allowed the Manchu forces through the pass and joined them, enabling the Qing conquest of China.

wu-zetian.s: Wu Zetian was the only woman to rule China as emperor in her own right, reigning from 690 to 705. A consort of the Tang emperors Taizong and Gaozong, she wielded power as empress and regent before proclaiming her own Zhou dynasty.

wu-zhou.s: Wu Zhou was the dynasty proclaimed by Wu Zetian in 690, which interrupted Tang rule until 705. Named Zhou after the ancient dynasty, it is known to historians as Wu Zhou to distinguish it.

wuchang.s: Wuchang is a historic city on the Yangtze River in central China, now part of the city of Wuhan. On 10 October 1911 a military mutiny there triggered the Xinhai Revolution.

wuzurg-framadar.s: The wuzurg framadar was the chief minister of the Sasanian Empire, often described as its grand vizier. The Sasanian Empire profile explains that he coordinated central administration beneath the Shahanshah.

wuzurgan.s: The wuzurgan were the great noble houses of the Sasanian Empire, whose military power and regional authority the dynasty could not entirely suppress. The Sasanian Empire profile describes how Sasanian administration combined the centralising ambitions of its founders with the…

wilfred-the-hairy.s: Wilfred the Hairy was Count of Urgell and Cerdanya from 870 and of Barcelona and Girona from 878, ruling most of the Catalan counties of the Spanish March. He resettled the depopulated plain of Vic and founded the monastery of Ripoll.

william-iv-of-the-united-kingdom.n: William IV of the United Kingdom
william-iv-of-the-united-kingdom.s: William IV was king of the United Kingdom and of Hanover from 1830 to 1837, a son of George III who had served in the Royal Navy. His reign saw the Reform Act of 1832 and the abolition of slavery in the British Empire.

william-iv-prince-of-orange.s: William IV, Prince of Orange, was a prince of the Nassau-Dietz line who inherited the Orange claims and gathered all the lands of the Nassau-Ottonian branch by 1743. During the French invasion of 1747 he was made hereditary stadtholder of all the provinces of the Dutch Republic.

william-iv-landgrave-of-hesse-kassel.s: William IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel, called the Wise, was the eldest son of Philip the Magnanimous. In the division of Hesse in 1567 he received about half the land, with Kassel as his capital.

wang-jingwei.s: Wang Jingwei was a leading figure of the Chinese Nationalist Party, a close associate of Sun Yat-sen and a rival of Chiang Kai-shek. In 1938 he broke with Chiang and sought peace with Japan, and in 1940 he became head of a Japanese-sponsored Reorganised National Government at…

west-pakistan.s: West Pakistan was the single province formed in 1955 under the One Unit scheme by merging the provinces and princely states of the western wing of Pakistan, including Punjab, Sindh, the North-West Frontier, Baluchistan, Bahawalpur, Khairpur and the Baluchistan States Union.…

west-indies-associated-states.s: The West Indies Associated States was the collective name for British colonies in the eastern Caribbean that became states in free association with the United Kingdom under the West Indies Act 1967. Each had full internal self-government, while Britain kept responsibility for…

william-iii-of-england.s: William III, Prince of Orange, became stadtholder of Holland in 1672, when France invaded the Dutch Republic, and led the resistance to Louis XIV. In 1688 he invaded England, and in 1689 he and his wife Mary II were proclaimed joint monarchs of England, Scotland and Ireland.

william-iii-duke-of-bavaria.s: William III was Duke of Bavaria-Munich, ruling jointly with his brother Ernest after their father John II died in 1397. The brothers defended their share against their cousins of Bavaria-Ingolstadt and in 1429 received part of the Duchy of Bavaria-Straubing.

william-penn.s: William Penn was an English Quaker and the founder of the Province of Pennsylvania. Son of the admiral Sir William Penn, he became a trustee of West Jersey and a proprietor of East Jersey, and in 1681 Charles II granted him a vast colony west of the Delaware River to settle a…

wessex.s: Wessex was the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of the West Saxons in southern England, centred on Winchester. From the 9th century it absorbed Kent, Sussex, Surrey and Cornwall, and under Alfred the Great it alone survived the Viking conquests.

william-ii-of-holland.s: William II of Holland was Count of Holland from 1234 and was elected King of the Romans in 1247 by princes opposed to the Hohenstaufen emperor Frederick II. He began building the Binnenhof at The Hague as his residence.

william-ii-elector-of-hesse.s: William II, Elector of Hesse, ruled the Electorate of Hesse-Kassel from 1821. His autocratic rule and quarrels with his family provoked unrest, and after the revolution of 1830 he accepted a constitution and left government to his son Frederick William as co-regent.

william-ii-of-wurttemberg.s: William II of Württemberg was the last King of Württemberg, reigning from 1891 to 1918. A popular and unpretentious constitutional monarch, he ruled his kingdom as a member state of the German Empire.

william-ii-duke-of-apulia.s: William II, Duke of Apulia, was the grandson of Robert Guiscard and ruled the Norman duchy of Apulia and Calabria from 1111. His reign was weakened by rebellious barons and he depended on his cousin Roger II of Sicily.

william-the-conqueror.s: William the Conqueror was Duke of Normandy from 1035 and King of England from 1066, after defeating Harold II at Hastings. He crushed English revolts, replaced the Anglo-Saxon elite with Norman lords and created powerful frontier earldoms such as Chester.

william-duke-of-julich-cleves-berg.s: William, Duke of Jülich-Cleves-Berg, known as William the Rich, ruled the United Duchies on the Lower Rhine from 1539. His claim to Guelders led to war with Emperor Charles V, who forced him to give it up by the Treaty of Venlo in 1543.

william-i-count-of-nassau-siegen.s: William I, Count of Nassau-Siegen, also called William the Rich, ruled the German lands of the house of Nassau from Dillenburg. He introduced the Lutheran Reformation in his territories.

william-the-silent.s: William the Silent, Prince of Orange from 1544, was born at Dillenburg into the house of Nassau. He led the Dutch Revolt against Philip II of Spain from 1568, and the northern provinces renounced Philip in 1581.

warring-states-period.s: The Warring States period was the final phase of the Eastern Zhou in ancient China, when seven major states, Qin, Chu, Qi, Yan, Han, Zhao and Wei, fought for supremacy. It saw mass infantry armies, iron tools, legalist reforms and the work of thinkers such as Mencius and…

white-volta.s: The White Volta is a river of West Africa that rises in northern Burkina Faso and flows south into Ghana, where it joins the Black Volta to form the Volta, now dammed as Lake Volta. Its valley was the heartland of the Mossi kingdoms and of Dagbon, and it linked the savanna…

william-i-of-sicily.s: William I of Sicily, called the Bad, was King of Sicily from 1154 to 1166, succeeding his father Roger II. His reign faced baronial revolts and a Byzantine invasion of Apulia, which he defeated in 1156.

william-i-of-wurttemberg.s: William I was King of Württemberg from 1816 until his death in 1864. He granted a constitution in 1819 that established a two-chamber diet, and promoted farming through the agricultural academy at Hohenheim and the Cannstatter Wasen festival.

william-i-elector-of-hesse.s: William I, Elector of Hesse, ruled Hesse-Kassel as Landgrave William IX from 1785 and became an elector in 1803. His wealth came largely from hiring out soldiers to Britain.

william-marshal-1st-earl-of-pembroke.s: William Marshal was an English knight who served four Angevin kings and became famous as a tournament champion. His marriage to the heiress Isabel de Clare in 1189 brought him Pembroke and the lordship of Leinster, where he founded towns such as New Ross.

wang-jian-qin.s: Wang Jian was a general of the state of Qin under King Zheng, the future First Emperor. He conquered Zhao and, after an earlier Qin army had failed, led a force of some 600,000 men against Chu, destroying it in 223 BCE.

wang-jian-former-shu.s: Wang Jian was a soldier of humble origin who rose in the Tang army and became military governor in Sichuan, taking Chengdu in 891. After the Tang fell in 907 he proclaimed himself emperor of Former Shu.

wang-mang.s: Wang Mang was a Han court official and relative of the empress dowager who seized the throne in 9 CE and founded the Xin dynasty. He attempted sweeping reforms, nationalising land, abolishing private slavery and reissuing coinage.

wang-shenzhi.s: Wang Shenzhi was the founder of the state of Min in Fujian. He came south with his brother's rebel army and ruled Fujian from 898, receiving the title Prince of Min in 909 from the Later Liang.

wang-shichong.s: Wang Shichong was a Sui general who held Luoyang during the dynasty's collapse. In 619 he deposed the Sui emperor Yang Tong and proclaimed his own state of Zheng.

wei-bao.s: Wei Bao was a member of the royal house of Wei who joined the rising against the Qin dynasty. In 206 BCE Xiang Yu made him King of Western Wei in southern Shanxi.

wei-river.s: The Wei River is the main tributary of the Yellow River, flowing east through Gansu and Shaanxi in northern China. Its valley, the Guanzhong plain, was the homeland of the Zhou and the Qin and the site of the capitals Hao, Xianyang and Chang'an.

wei-river-shandong.s: The Wei River of Shandong is a river of the Shandong peninsula in eastern China, flowing north into the Bohai Sea. In 203 BCE the Han general Han Xin won a battle on it against the army of Qi and its Chu allies under Long Ju, by releasing water held back with sandbags.

western-dvina.s: The Western Dvina, called the Daugava in Latvia, rises in the Valdai Hills of Russia and flows through Belarus and Latvia to the Gulf of Riga. In the early Middle Ages it was a trade route linking the Baltic with Rus', settled by the Krivichs.

william-count-of-schaumburg-lippe.s: William was count of Schaumburg-Lippe from 1748 to 1777 and a noted military reformer of the Enlightenment. He commanded the Allied artillery in the Seven Years' War and in 1762 reorganised the Portuguese army against a Spanish invasion.

william-duke-of-nassau.s: William was duke of Nassau from 1816 to 1839, uniting the lands of the Nassau-Weilburg and Nassau-Usingen lines. He granted one of the first constitutions in the German states in 1814 but ruled in an authoritarian style and quarrelled with the estates over the ducal domains.

william-howard-taft.s: William Howard Taft was an American lawyer and politician who headed the Philippine Commission from 1900 and became the first civilian governor-general of the Philippines in 1901. As secretary of war he briefly served as provisional governor of Cuba in 1906.

william-i-duke-of-aquitaine.s: William the Pious was count of Auvergne and, from 893, duke of Aquitaine, one of the greatest nobles of the late Carolingian kingdom. In 910 he founded the abbey of Cluny in Burgundy, freeing it from lay control and placing it under the pope, and it became the centre of a…

william-walker.s: William Walker was an American filibuster from Tennessee. In 1853 he raided Baja California and proclaimed a short-lived Republic of Lower California.

wladyslaw-i-lokietek.s: Władysław I Łokietek, 'the Elbow-high', was a Piast duke of Kuyavia who spent decades fighting rival dukes, Bohemia and the Teutonic Knights for the fragmented Polish lands. He held smaller duchies such as Brześć Kujawski, Łęczyca and Sieradz on his way to power, and in 1320…

wolter-von-plettenberg.s: Wolter von Plettenberg was Master of the Livonian Order from 1494 to 1535 and the leading figure of the Livonian Confederation. His victory over Muscovite forces at Smolino in 1502 secured half a century of peace on the eastern frontier.

william-i-of-angouleme.s: William I of Angoulême, called Taillefer, was a 10th-century count of Angoulême in western France. Tradition gives him his nickname, 'iron-cutter', from a blow that split a Viking's armour.

william-i-duke-of-julich.s: William I, Duke of Jülich, ruled Jülich as Count William V from 1328. An ally of Emperor Louis IV and brother-in-law of Edward III of England, he was made a margrave in 1336 and raised to duke by Emperor Charles IV in 1356.

war-of-the-landshut-succession.s: The War of the Landshut Succession was fought in 1503–1505 over the Duchy of Bavaria-Landshut. Duke George the Rich had left his lands to his son-in-law Rupert of the Palatinate in breach of Wittelsbach family agreements, and Albert IV of Bavaria-Munich went to war.

wadi-bayhan.s: Wadi Bayhan is a valley in the interior of south-western Yemen, opening onto the edge of the Ramlat al-Sab'atayn desert. In antiquity it was the heart of the Kingdom of Qataban, whose capital Timna lay there at the start of the incense caravan route, with extensive irrigation…

wali-songo.s: The Wali Songo, or 'nine saints', are the Muslim teachers revered in Javanese tradition for spreading Islam in Java in the 15th and 16th centuries. Among them were Sunan Ampel, Sunan Giri, Sunan Kalijaga and Sunan Gunung Jati; several founded religious schools or ruling…

wang-kemin.s: Wang Kemin was a Chinese banker and former finance minister of the Beiyang government who collaborated with Japan after its invasion of northern China. In December 1937 he became head of the Provisional Government of the Republic of China in Beijing, which in 1940 was absorbed…

wang-on.s: Wang On was a member of the Goryeo royal family proclaimed king by the Sambyeolcho, the elite military units that rebelled in 1270 when King Wonjong ended military rule and accepted Mongol overlordship. With the rebel leader Bae Jung-son he held Jindo island off south-western…

wang-yan-former-shu.s: Wang Yan was the second and last emperor of Former Shu, one of the Ten Kingdoms, in Sichuan, succeeding his father Wang Jian in 918. Pleasure-loving and extravagant, he left government to favourites.

wat-phu.s: Wat Phu is a ruined Khmer temple complex in Champasak province in southern Laos, built at the foot of a mountain whose summit resembles a linga. A Shaivite sanctuary from around the 5th century, rebuilt mainly in the 11th and 12th centuries, it is linked to the early Chenla…

west-indies.s: The West Indies are the islands of the Caribbean Sea, from the Bahamas and the Greater Antilles to the Lesser Antilles, named after Columbus's belief that he had reached Asia. From the 16th century Spain, Britain, France, the Netherlands and Denmark built sugar colonies there…

western-regions.s: The Western Regions was the Chinese name, from the Han dynasty, for the lands west of the Yumen Pass, chiefly the oasis city-states of the Tarim Basin such as Kucha, Karasahr, Khotan and Shule. Han China contested them with the Xiongnu from the 2nd century BCE and set up a…

white-australia-policy.s: The White Australia policy was the set of laws and practices, beginning with the Immigration Restriction Act of 1901, by which the new Commonwealth of Australia excluded non-European immigrants, chiefly through a dictation test. Pacific Islander labourers in Queensland's sugar…

white-terror-hungary.s: The White Terror in Hungary was a wave of counter-revolutionary violence in 1919–1921 after the fall of the Hungarian Soviet Republic. Officer detachments of Miklós Horthy's National Army killed, imprisoned and tortured thousands of suspected communists, socialists and Jews.

widukind-of-corvey.s: Widukind of Corvey was a Saxon monk of the abbey of Corvey and author of the Deeds of the Saxons (Res gestae Saxonicae), written in the late 960s and early 970s. It is a chief source for the Ottonian kings Henry the Fowler and Otto I, including Otto's victory at the Lechfeld…

wilhelm-adolf-count-of-rantzau.s: Wilhelm Adolf was the last Count of Rantzau, an imperial county in Holstein. In 1721 his brother Count Christian Detlev was shot dead, and Wilhelm Adolf was arrested and convicted of arranging the killing.

william-prince-of-albania.s: William, Prince of Albania, born Prince Wilhelm of Wied, was a German officer chosen by the Great Powers in 1913 as ruler of the new Principality of Albania. He arrived at Durrës in March 1914 but faced rebellion in central Albania, rivalry with Essad Pasha Toptani and the…

william-ii-of-villehardouin.s: William II of Villehardouin was Prince of Achaea in the Frankish Morea from 1246 to 1278. He completed the conquest of the Peloponnese with the fall of Monemvasia in 1248 and built castles such as Mistras and Grand Magne.

william-of-modena.s: William of Modena was an Italian churchman and papal legate in the Baltic lands from the 1220s. He mediated between the Danes, the Livonian Order and the local converts in Livonia and Estonia and helped bring about the Treaty of Stensby in 1238.

william-sayle.s: William Sayle was an English Puritan colonist and governor of Bermuda who in 1648 led the Eleutheran Adventurers, settlers from Bermuda seeking religious freedom, to found a colony on Eleuthera in the Bahamas. In old age he was appointed the first governor of the Province of…

wizlaw-iii-prince-of-rugen.s: Wizlaw III was the last Prince of Rügen of the native Slavic dynasty, ruling from 1302 to 1325 under Danish overlordship over the island and the mainland around Stralsund. He is known as a minnesinger, whose German love songs survive in the Jena song manuscript.

wladyslaw-ii-the-exile.s: Władysław II the Exile was the eldest son of Bolesław III Wrymouth and, under his father's testament of 1138, High Duke of Poland and Duke of Silesia. His attempt to dispossess his younger half-brothers failed, and in 1146 they drove him into exile in Germany, where he died in…

woodes-rogers.s: Woodes Rogers was an English privateer and colonial governor who sailed round the world in 1708–1711, rescuing the castaway Alexander Selkirk on the way. Appointed first royal governor of the Bahamas, he arrived at Nassau in 1718 with a royal pardon, broke up the pirates'…

wu-rui.s: Wu Rui was a Qin magistrate of Po county, popular with the Yue peoples of the south, who joined the rebellion against the Qin dynasty with his son-in-law Ying Bu. In 206 BCE Xiang Yu made him King of Hengshan in the middle Yangtze, but he supported Liu Bang, and after the Han…

war-of-the-austrian-succession.s: The War of the Austrian Succession was a European war fought from 1740 to 1748 over Maria Theresa's right to inherit the Habsburg lands after the death of Emperor Charles VI. Prussia under Frederick the Great seized most of Silesia, and the Bavarian elector Charles Albert was…

walter-of-geroldseck.s: Walter of Geroldseck was Bishop of Strasbourg from 1260. He tried to restore episcopal control over the city's government, but its citizens defeated his army at the Battle of Hausbergen in 1262.

william-iii-duke-of-aquitaine.s: William III, Duke of Aquitaine, called Towhead, was count of Poitou from 935 and duke of Aquitaine from about 959 until his death in 963. Of the Ramnulfid family, he claimed the ducal title against the counts of Toulouse and Auvergne, and from his time the counts of Poitou…

william-iii-count-of-nevers.s: William III, Count of Nevers, ruled Nevers, Auxerre and Tonnerre from 1148 until his death in 1161. He took part in the Second Crusade with Louis VII of France from 1147 and quarrelled with the abbey of Vézelay over his rights in the town.

william-ix-duke-of-aquitaine.s: William IX, Duke of Aquitaine and Count of Poitou, is the earliest troubadour whose works survive, composing lyric poetry in Occitan. A powerful and often excommunicated prince, he led an army on the crusade of 1101 and fought in Spain.

wolfgang-count-palatine-of-zweibrucken.s: Wolfgang, Count Palatine of Zweibrücken, was a Wittelsbach prince who introduced the Lutheran Reformation in his lands and inherited Palatinate-Neuburg in 1557. By the Treaty of Marburg in 1543 he ceded Veldenz to his uncle Rupert.

william-donn-de-burgh-3rd-earl-of-ulster.n: William Donn de Burgh, 3rd Earl of Ulster
william-donn-de-burgh-3rd-earl-of-ulster.s: William Donn de Burgh, 3rd Earl of Ulster, the 'Brown Earl', was the Anglo-Norman lord of Ulster and much of Connacht. His murder by his own followers at Carrickfergus in 1333 left only an infant daughter, and his kinsmen seized the de Burgh lands in Connacht, founding the…

war-of-the-eight-princes.s: The War of the Eight Princes was a series of civil wars among princes of the Sima family of the Western Jin dynasty, fought from 291 to 306 for control of the mentally incapable Emperor Hui. Triggered by Empress Jia's intrigues, it devastated northern China and exhausted the…

wenceslaus-iv-of-bohemia.s: Wenceslaus IV of Bohemia, son of Emperor Charles IV, was King of Bohemia from 1378 and King of the Romans from 1376 until the electors deposed him in 1400. In 1395 he sold Gian Galeazzo Visconti the title of Duke of Milan, one of the grievances behind his deposition.

william-i-of-the-netherlands.s: William I was the first King of the Netherlands, reigning from 1815 to 1840. A son of William V, the last stadtholder, and great-grandson of William IV of Orange-Nassau-Diez, he ruled the United Kingdom of the Netherlands, including present-day Belgium.

war-of-the-mantuan-succession.s: The War of the Mantuan Succession was fought after the main Gonzaga line died out in 1627. France backed the claim of Charles Gonzaga, Duke of Nevers, to Mantua and Montferrat, while Spain, Savoy and the Holy Roman Emperor opposed him.

william-stapleton-1st-baronet.s: Sir William Stapleton, 1st Baronet, was an Irish soldier and governor-in-chief of the Leeward Islands from 1672 to 1686. He organised the separate Leeward Islands government of Antigua, Saint Kitts, Nevis and Montserrat, called its general assembly and built up their defences…

war-of-the-thuringian-succession.s: The War of the Thuringian Succession of 1247–1264 followed the death without heirs of Henry Raspe, the last Ludowingian landgrave of Thuringia. Henry the Illustrious, Margrave of Meissen, fought Sophie of Brabant, daughter of Landgrave Louis IV, for the inheritance.

wadi-allaqi.s: Wadi Allaqi is a long dry valley in the Eastern Desert of southern Egypt, running from the Red Sea Hills towards the Nile south of Aswan. It held the richest gold mines of ancient Nubia, worked by Egypt in the New Kingdom and later by the Banu Kanz chiefs under the Fatimids.

wadi-markha.s: Wadi Markha is a valley in southern Yemen, south-west of the inland incense-route valleys. It was the heartland of the ancient Kingdom of Awsan, whose power Saba broke in the 7th century BCE, and later lay within the reach of the Kingdom of Qataban at its height.

wahsudan-ibn-marzuban.s: Wahsudan ibn Marzuban was a ruler of the Justanid dynasty of Daylam in the mountains of northern Iran in the 9th century. Tradition credits him with building the castle of Alamut around 860, the fortress that later became the headquarters of the Nizari Ismailis under Hasan-i…

wajid-ali-shah.s: Wajid Ali Shah was the last King of Awadh, reigning from 1847 to 1856. A poet and patron of music and Kathak dance, he was deposed when Governor-General Dalhousie annexed Awadh in 1856, alleging misrule, and spent the rest of his life in exile at Metiabruz near Calcutta.

wajih-al-din-masud.s: Wajih al-Din Mas'ud was the second leader of the Sarbadars of western Khurasan, succeeding his brother Abd al-Razzaq in 1338. He took Sabzevar and Nishapur and defeated the Ilkhanid claimant Togha Temür, building the Sarbadar state, but was killed in 1344 during a campaign…

walter-de-lacy-lord-of-meath.n: Walter de Lacy, Lord of Meath
walter-de-lacy-lord-of-meath.s: Walter de Lacy was an Anglo-Norman baron and Lord of Meath in Ireland, son of Hugh de Lacy. He lost his Irish lands in a conflict with King John in 1210 but recovered the lordship and held it until his death in 1241, after which Meath was divided between his granddaughters.

walter-lini.s: Walter Lini was an Anglican priest and the leader of the Vanua'aku Pati, which led the New Hebrides to independence from Anglo-French rule. He became the first Prime Minister of Vanuatu in 1980, holding office until 1991, after Papua New Guinean troops helped end the Santo…

walter-v-of-brienne.s: Walter V of Brienne was Duke of Athens from 1308. He hired the Catalan Company against his Byzantine and Thessalian rivals, but when he refused to pay them they killed him and most of his knights at the Battle of Halmyros in 1311, taking the duchy; his heirs kept only Argos…

walter-of-rosieres.s: Walter of Rosières was a Frankish knight who took part in the conquest of the Peloponnese after the Fourth Crusade. Around 1209 he received the barony of Akova, one of the twelve original baronies of the Principality of Achaea, with 24 knight's fiefs in the mountains of Arcadia.

walter-patterson.s: Walter Patterson was an Irish-born British officer who became the first governor of St John's Island, later Prince Edward Island, when it was made a separate colony in 1769. His long quarrels with the absentee proprietors over land and quit-rents led to his recall in 1786.

walter-von-cronberg.s: Walter von Cronberg was German Master of the Teutonic Order at Mergentheim. After Grand Master Albert secularised Prussia in 1525, the emperor made him administrator of the grand mastership in 1527, and his successors combined the two offices, ruling the order's remaining…

wang-meng-former-qin.s: Wang Meng was the Han Chinese chief minister of Fu Jian, ruler of the Former Qin in northern China. He built an effective Chinese-style administration, promoted Confucian learning and agriculture, and in 370 led the campaign that took Ye and captured the Former Yan emperor…

wang-yanjun.s: Wang Yanjun was a son of Wang Shenzhi, founder of the Min kingdom in Fujian. He seized power in 926 and in 933 proclaimed himself emperor, breaking with the northern dynasties, but his extravagant rule ended when he was murdered in a palace coup in 935, the first of a series…

war-jabi.s: War Jabi was a ruler of Takrur in the middle Senegal valley and one of the first West African kings to adopt Islam, according to the geographer al-Bakri. He imposed Islamic law on his subjects, and his son Labi fought alongside the Almoravids against the Gudala in 1056.

warren-hastings.s: Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General of Bengal, heading the East India Company's administration in India from 1773 to 1785. He reorganised revenue and justice, fought the Marathas and Mysore, and patronised oriental learning.

wat-xieng-thong.s: Wat Xieng Thong is a Buddhist temple in Luang Prabang, Laos, built in 1559–1560 under King Setthathirath of Lan Xang. With its sweeping tiered roofs it is the finest example of the Luang Prabang style, and it remained a centre of royal ceremony for the later Kingdom of Luang…

waththab-ibn-sabiq.s: Waththab ibn Sabiq al-Numayri was the founder of the Numayrid emirate of the Banu Numayr tribe in the Diyar Mudar region of Upper Mesopotamia. As Hamdanid power faded he seized Harran around 990, and his tribe went on to hold Saruj, Raqqa and for a time Edessa.

watul-katel.s: Wat'ul K'atel was a Maya lord of Ceibal in Guatemala, installed in 829 under the patronage of Ucanal. Ceibal revived under him after the collapse of the Petexbatun kingdom, and his stelae show foreign-looking dress and new artistic styles, perhaps linked to the Gulf Coast or…

waxaklajuun-ubaah-kawiil.s: Waxaklajuun Ub'aah K'awiil, often called 18 Rabbit, was the thirteenth king of the Maya city of Copán. He commissioned the deeply carved stelae of the Great Plaza and the ball court, but in 738 he was captured and beheaded by his former vassal K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat of Quiriguá.

weizi.s: Weizi Qi was an elder brother of Di Xin, the last king of the Shang dynasty. After the failed rebellion of Wu Geng, the Duke of Zhou installed him at Shangqiu as ruler of the new state of Song, so that the sacrifices to the Shang royal ancestors would continue.

wenceslaus-ii-of-bohemia.s: Wenceslaus II was King of Bohemia from 1278 and King of Poland from 1300. Enriched by the silver of Kutná Hora, where he introduced the Prague groschen, he extended Bohemian overlordship over the Silesian duchies and won Greater Poland and Kraków, uniting Poland under his rule…

wenceslaus-of-plock.s: Wenceslaus of Płock was a Piast Duke of Płock in Masovia from 1313. Caught between Poland, Bohemia and the Teutonic Order, he allied with the Knights and in 1329 did homage to John of Bohemia, making Płock a Bohemian fief in opposition to the Polish king Władysław the Elbow-high.

wenzel-anton-von-kaunitz-rietberg.s: Wenzel Anton von Kaunitz-Rietberg was state chancellor of the Habsburg monarchy from 1753 to 1792 under Maria Theresa, Joseph II and Leopold II. He engineered the alliance with France of 1756, the Diplomatic Revolution, and his family held the small Westphalian County of…

west-bank.s: The West Bank is the territory west of the Jordan River that was part of Mandatory Palestine. In the 1948 war Jordan's Arab Legion held it together with East Jerusalem, and Jordan annexed both in 1950; Israel occupied the territory in the war of 1967, and its status remains at…

west-prussia.s: West Prussia was a province of the Kingdom of Prussia formed from most of Royal Prussia, which Prussia gained from Poland in the First Partition of 1772; Gdańsk and Toruń followed in 1793. Its capital was Danzig, and after the First World War most of the province went to…

western-india-states-agency.s: The Western India States Agency was a political agency of British India, formed in 1924 to oversee the many princely states of Kathiawar, Cutch and parts of Gujarat through a single agent to the Governor-General at Rajkot. Its states, among them Manavadar and Radhanpur, joined…

western-sahara.s: Western Sahara is a sparsely populated desert territory on the Atlantic coast of north-west Africa, formerly the Spanish Sahara. Its Sanhaja Berber nomads gave rise to the Almoravid movement in the 11th century.

western-schism.s: The Western Schism was a split in the Catholic Church from 1378 to 1417, when rival popes in Rome and Avignon, and from 1409 a third line from Pisa, each claimed the papacy with the backing of different kingdoms. The Council of Constance ended it by deposing or accepting the…

western-thrace.s: Western Thrace is the region between the Nestos and Evros rivers in north-eastern Greece. Taken by Bulgaria in the First Balkan War, it saw a short-lived Muslim-led provisional government in 1913, passed to Greece after the First World War, and its Muslim minority was exempted…

white-nile.s: The White Nile is the longer of the two main branches of the Nile, flowing north from the Great Lakes region through South Sudan to meet the Blue Nile at Khartoum. The Shilluk kingdom lay along its banks, and in the 19th century Turco-Egyptian merchants opened it to the ivory…

wilhelm-frick.s: Wilhelm Frick was a leading Nazi politician. In 1930 he became interior minister of Thuringia, the first Nazi to hold a ministerial post in Germany, and from 1933 to 1943 he was Reich Minister of the Interior, drafting laws that centralised the state and the Nuremberg race laws.

wilhelm-hartwig-beseler.s: Wilhelm Hartwig Beseler was a lawyer and leader of the German national movement in Schleswig-Holstein. In March 1848 he headed, with Prince Frederick of Noer, the provisional government at Kiel that claimed both duchies for the German Confederation, starting the First…

wilhelm-murr.s: Wilhelm Murr was the Nazi Gauleiter of Württemberg-Hohenzollern and, from 1933, Reich governor of Württemberg, where he also headed the state government. He ruled the state until the end of the Second World War and killed himself in May 1945.

wilhelm-of-brandenburg.s: Wilhelm of Brandenburg was the last Archbishop of Riga, a brother of Duke Albert of Prussia. During the Livonian War he placed his lands under Polish-Lithuanian protection, and in 1561–1562 the archbishopric was secularised and incorporated into the Duchy of Livonia under…

william-aleman.s: William Aleman was a Frankish knight, possibly of German or Provençal origin, who became the first Baron of Patras when the Principality of Achaea was organised around 1209. His barony of 24 knight's fiefs held the main port of the north-western Peloponnese, which he held as a…

william-augustus-bowles.s: William Augustus Bowles was a Maryland-born Loyalist adventurer who married into the Muscogee Confederacy. After escaping Spanish captivity he returned to Florida in 1799 and proclaimed the State of Muskogee, which challenged Spain for four years until he was betrayed to the…

william-bolts.s: William Bolts was a Dutch-born merchant and former servant of the British East India Company, expelled from Bengal after quarrels with its government. He persuaded the Austria of Maria Theresa to back a trading venture to Africa and Asia, and in 1777 founded the short-lived…

william-bradford-governor.s: William Bradford was a Pilgrim leader who sailed on the Mayflower in 1620 and was governor of Plymouth Colony for most years from 1621 until 1657. His history Of Plymouth Plantation is the main source for the colony's founding and early years.

william-de-braose-4th-lord-of-bramber.n: William de Braose, 4th Lord of Bramber
william-de-braose-4th-lord-of-bramber.s: William de Braose, 4th Lord of Bramber, was a powerful Anglo-Norman marcher lord in Wales who held Brecknock through his mother and received Gower from King John in 1203. Notorious for the massacre of Welsh chiefs at Abergavenny in 1175, he later fell from John's favour and…

william-franklin.s: William Franklin was the son of Benjamin Franklin and the last royal governor of New Jersey, from 1763 to 1776. He remained loyal to the Crown during the American Revolution, was arrested in 1776, and after his release led Loyalist associations in New York before settling in…

william-henry-prince-of-nassau-saarbruck.s: William Henry was Prince of Nassau-Saarbrücken from 1741. With his architect Friedrich Joachim Stengel he rebuilt Saarbrücken as a Baroque residence, and he promoted coal mining and ironworks in the Saar, laying foundations for the region's later industry.

william-henry-duke-of-saxe-eisenach.s: William Henry was the last Duke of Saxe-Eisenach, ruling from 1729 to 1741. He died without heirs, and the duchy passed to his kinsman Ernest Augustus I of Saxe-Weimar, who united the two lands as Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach, a union that lasted until the end of the German monarchies…

william-ii-of-sicily.s: William II, called the Good, was the Norman King of Sicily from 1166 to 1189. His fleets campaigned against Byzantium, taking Cephalonia and Zakynthos and sacking Thessalonica in 1185, and supported Isaac Komnenos in Cyprus.

william-iii-of-the-netherlands.s: William III was King of the Netherlands, Grand Duke of Luxembourg and, until 1866, Duke of Limburg in the German Confederation, reigning from 1849 to 1890. He reluctantly accepted the liberal constitution of 1848 and the limits on royal power it brought.

william-iv-of-forcalquier.s: William IV was the last independent Count of Forcalquier in Provence. In 1193 his granddaughter Garsenda married Alfonso II of Provence, and on William's death in 1209 Forcalquier was reunited with the County of Provence under the house of Barcelona.

william-macgregor.s: William MacGregor was a Scottish physician and colonial governor. As administrator of British New Guinea from 1888 to 1898 he explored the interior, set up government stations, appointed village constables and restricted land sales to Europeans, foundations later taken over by…

william-mackinnon.s: William Mackinnon was a Scottish shipping magnate, founder of the British India Steam Navigation Company. He founded the Imperial British East Africa Company, which received a royal charter in 1888 to administer the British sphere in East Africa, and backed the expedition to…

william-milton.s: William Milton was a British colonial administrator and cricketer who served as Administrator of Southern Rhodesia for the British South Africa Company from 1898 to 1914. He organised the civil service of the company's territory and oversaw the growth of settler farming and…

william-montagu-1st-earl-of-salisbury.s: William Montagu, 1st Earl of Salisbury, was a close companion of Edward III who helped him overthrow Roger Mortimer in 1330. From 1333 the king granted him the lordship of the Isle of Man, which he secured against Scottish claims, beginning permanent English rule over the island.

william-of-werle.s: William of Werle was the last Lord of Werle, a Mecklenburg lordship ruled by a branch of the Nikloting dynasty. He died in 1436 without a son, and his lands passed to the Dukes of Mecklenburg, completing the reunion of the Mecklenburg territories.

william-paterson-banker.s: William Paterson was a Scottish trader and banker, a founder of the Bank of England in 1694. He promoted the Company of Scotland's Darien scheme to found a colony on the Isthmus of Panama linking the Atlantic and Pacific trades; he sailed with the expedition in 1698 and…

william-prout-maryland.s: William Prout was a settler leader of the colony of Maryland in Africa at Cape Palmas, founded by the Maryland State Colonization Society. When the colony declared independence as the Republic of Maryland in 1854 he became its first governor; the republic was annexed by…

william-shirley.s: William Shirley was a British lawyer and governor of the Province of Massachusetts Bay from 1741 to 1749 and 1753 to 1756. He organised the New England expedition that captured the French fortress of Louisbourg in 1745 and briefly commanded British forces in North America in…

william-i-of-provence.s: William I of Provence, called the Liberator, was Count of Provence from about 968. In 973 he drove the Saracens from their base at Fraxinetum, ending decades of raids, and distributed the recovered lands to his followers, becoming effective ruler of the region and founding the…

william-tryon.s: William Tryon was a British army officer and colonial governor of North Carolina from 1765 to 1771 and of New York from 1771 to 1780. In North Carolina he built Tryon Palace at New Bern and crushed the Regulator movement at Alamance in 1771; in the Revolutionary War he led…

william-tubman.s: William Tubman was President of Liberia from 1944 until his death in 1971, the longest-serving president in its history. His open-door policy brought foreign investment in iron ore and rubber, and his unification policy extended rights to the indigenous majority, though power…

william-worthington-jordan.s: William Worthington Jordan was a Cape Colony trader and explorer in south-western Africa. In 1885 he bought land around Grootfontein from the Ndonga king Kambonde for the Dorsland trekkers, who founded the Republic of Upingtonia there; he was murdered in Ovamboland in 1886 and…

winston-churchill.s: Winston Churchill was a British statesman and Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1940 to 1945 and 1951 to 1955, leading Britain through the Second World War. As colonial secretary at the Cairo Conference of 1921 he agreed that Abdullah would govern Transjordan under…

wladyslaw-ii-of-opole.s: Władysław II of Opole, known as Opolczyk, was a Piast Duke of Opole in Silesia who served the Angevin kings as palatine of Hungary and governor of Galicia. In 1382 he founded the Pauline monastery of Jasna Góra at Częstochowa and brought there the Black Madonna icon, later…

wladyslaw-odonic.s: Władysław Odonic was a Piast Duke of Greater Poland who fought his uncle Władysław Spindleshanks for the duchy and won it after 1229. He relied on the support of the Archbishop of Gniezno, granting the church wide privileges, and his sons Przemysł I and Bolesław the Pious…

wladyslaw-of-bytom.s: Władysław of Bytom was a Silesian Piast duke who ruled Koźle and Bytom in the first half of the 14th century. Like the other Upper Silesian dukes he accepted the overlordship of John of Bohemia in 1327, bringing his duchies under the Bohemian crown.

wladyslaw-of-dobrzyn.s: Władysław of Dobrzyń, called the Humpback, was a Kuyavian Piast duke and nephew of King Władysław the Elbow-high. After Poland was reunited in 1320 he ruled Łęczyca as a duchy, exchanging it with his uncle for Dobrzyń in 1327, and later recovered Dobrzyń from the Teutonic Order.

wladyslaw-of-opole.s: Władysław of Opole was a Piast Duke of Opole and Racibórz in Upper Silesia from 1246 to 1281. He founded towns under German law and allied with Bohemia against the Hungarians.

wolf-dietrich-von-raitenau.s: Wolf Dietrich von Raitenau was Prince-Archbishop of Salzburg from 1587 to 1612. He began rebuilding the city in Italian baroque style, clearing space for a new cathedral and building the Mirabell palace for his companion Salome Alt, but after a conflict with Bavaria over salt…

wolfgang-william-count-palatine-of-neubu.n: Wolfgang William, Count Palatine of Neuburg
wolfgang-william-count-palatine-of-neubu.s: Wolfgang William was Count Palatine of Neuburg from 1614. He converted to Catholicism in 1613 to strengthen his claim in the Jülich succession dispute, and under the Treaty of Xanten of 1614 he won the duchies of Jülich and Berg, ruling from Düsseldorf.

workers-party-of-ethiopia.s: The Workers' Party of Ethiopia was the Marxist–Leninist ruling party founded by the Derg military regime in 1984, with Mengistu Haile Mariam as general secretary. Under the constitution of 1987 it became the leading force of the People's Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, and it…

world-trade-organization.s: The World Trade Organization is an international body founded in 1995 to succeed the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade and regulate trade between its members. China's entry in 2001 and Vietnam's in 2007 marked their integration into the world economy after decades of…

wu-guang.s: Wu Guang was, with Chen Sheng, a leader of the Dazexiang uprising of 209 BCE, the first great peasant rising in Chinese history. Conscripts held up by rain and facing death for lateness, they rebelled and founded the Zhangchu regime, which set the Qin empire ablaze; Wu Guang…

wu-han-general.s: Wu Han was a leading general of Emperor Guangwu, founder of the Eastern Han dynasty. With Cen Peng he advanced up the Yangtze against Gongsun Shu's Chengjia state in Sichuan, and in 36 he took and sacked Chengdu after Gongsun Shu was mortally wounded, completing the Han…

wu-shifan.s: Wu Shifan was the grandson of Wu Sangui and the last ruler of the Zhou regime set up during the Revolt of the Three Feudatories against the Qing. He succeeded in 1678, retreated to Kunming as Qing armies advanced, and killed himself when the city fell in 1681, ending the revolt.
